client: I've been really struggling since my surgery a few months ago — the medical bills just keep coming and I had no idea it was going to cost this much. Every time I check my mail or my bank account, I feel this wave of panic that I can't shake. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change the numbers on those bills, so I guess I'm a little doubtful about what therapy can actually do for me here.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're feeling this mix of dread and skepticism — you're dealing with something very real and stressful, and you're right that our conversations won't make those bills disappear. What therapy *can* do is help you work with the wave of panic that hits every time you open the mail, so it doesn't have the same grip on you, and help you think more clearly about your options rather than feeling frozen. What does that panic usually tell you in those moments — what's the thought that rushes in when you see a new bill?

client: The thought that rushes in is something like "this is never going to end" and "I'm going to lose everything." It's like my brain immediately jumps to the worst possible outcome — bankruptcy, losing my apartment, being completely alone with no way out. I know logically that probably won't happen, but in that moment it feels completely certain and I can't talk myself out of it.
therapist: That moment where the worst-case scenario feels completely certain — even when part of you knows it's not — is actually one of the most important things CBT can help with, and you've already taken a huge step by noticing that gap between what you *feel* and what you *know*. Those thoughts like "this will never end" and "I'll lose everything" are what we call catastrophic thinking, and they're incredibly common when we're under real financial stress — your brain is trying to protect you by scanning for danger, but it ends up amplifying the threat beyond what the evidence actually supports. When you say you "know logically it probably won't happen," what evidence are you actually holding onto that tells you things might not go as far as bankruptcy or losing your home?

client: I guess the evidence is that I still have my job, even though it's not a great-paying one, and I've managed to pay rent every month so far even while some of these bills have been sitting there. And a coworker mentioned that hospitals usually have financial assistance programs, so it's not like there are literally zero options. But honestly, even saying that out loud, it doesn't really make the panic go away — like I know the facts but my body doesn't seem to care about them.
therapist: You've just done something really important — you named real, concrete evidence that contradicts the "I'll lose everything" story, and that takes genuine effort when you're in the middle of this. The disconnect you're describing, where your mind can see the facts but your body still sounds the alarm, is completely normal — our nervous system learned to react faster than our rational thinking, so the panic doesn't just switch off because we've updated our thoughts. What do you think it might feel like in those mailbox moments if you could pause and remind yourself of exactly what you just said — that you've kept the rent paid, you still have income, and there are options you haven't even tried yet?

client: Honestly, I want to say it would feel better, but I'm not sure I'd actually remember to do that in the moment — when the panic hits, it's like my brain goes completely blank and I forget everything I know. It's kind of embarrassing to admit that, but even right now thinking about it, I can feel a little of that tightness in my chest. I guess I'm skeptical that I'd have the presence of mind to pause and recite evidence to myself when I'm already spiraling.
therapist: Please don't feel embarrassed about that — what you're describing is actually how panic works for almost everyone, and it would be unrealistic to expect yourself to calmly recite evidence when your nervous system is in full alarm mode. That's exactly why in CBT we don't rely on willpower in the moment; instead, we build small, almost automatic anchors *before* the panic hits — things like a single phrase written on your phone or a brief grounding routine that interrupts the spiral before your mind goes blank. I'm curious, is there a moment in your day — maybe before you check the mail or your bank account — where you feel calm enough that we could start building one of those anchors together?

client: I think mornings are probably my calmest time, before I've had a chance to check anything — it's like there's a small window before the day's worries pile on. But I'm a little skeptical about the phrase idea, because it sounds like it could feel hollow or forced, like telling yourself "everything's fine" when it clearly isn't. I don't want something that feels fake — I guess I'd need it to actually mean something to me for it to have any chance of working.
therapist: Your skepticism here is actually really healthy — empty reassurances like "everything's fine" would be dishonest, and your brain would reject them instantly because they don't match reality. What tends to work much better is something grounded in truth you've already proven, like "I've kept the rent paid every month even through this" — not a positive spin, but a factual anchor that your own experience backs up. Given that morning window you mentioned, what's one true thing about how you've handled this situation so far that you actually believe, even a little?

client: I think the thing I actually believe is that I've been dealing with this alone for months and I haven't completely fallen apart, even though it's felt like I was going to. That's not nothing, I guess — like, I've been scared every single day but I've still been showing up to work and handling things. I'm just worried that even if I find a phrase that feels true, I'll use it once and then forget about it, or it'll stop feeling real after a while.
therapist: What you just said — that you've been scared every single day and still kept showing up — that's not a small thing, that's actually remarkable resilience, and it deserves to be recognized as real evidence of your strength rather than just "not falling apart." Your worry about the phrase fading or feeling mechanical over time is completely valid, which is why we'd want to weave it into a small morning routine rather than relying on memory alone — something as simple as writing it in a notebook or as a phone reminder during that calm window, so it stays alive and connected to your actual experience. What would it mean to you to start each day by deliberately acknowledging that you've already survived months of this fear — do you think that could feel different from just telling yourself things are okay?

client: I think it might feel different, yeah — because it's not pretending the fear isn't there, it's more like acknowledging that the fear and the showing up are both true at the same time. But I'll be honest, there's a part of me that feels almost uncomfortable sitting with that, like I don't quite deserve to call it resilience when I'm still such a mess about all of this. I guess I could try the phone reminder thing, but I'm worried I'll just start dismissing it the way I dismiss every other notification on my phone.
therapist: The way you just framed that — fear and showing up being true at the same time — is actually a really sophisticated insight, and it's worth pausing on the fact that you arrived at that yourself. The discomfort about "deserving" to call it resilience is something I'd gently push back on, because being a mess *and* still functioning isn't a contradiction that cancels out your strength — it's literally what resilience looks like in real life, not in a movie. For the phone reminder, what if instead of a generic notification you made it something specific enough that it would actually stop you — maybe the exact words you just used, about fear and showing up both being true?

client: Using my own words does feel less like a generic pep talk, I'll admit that. But I'm sitting here thinking, what if I read it and just feel nothing — like it becomes wallpaper after a few days, just another thing I scroll past? I don't want to set myself up to feel like I've failed at yet another thing on top of everything else I'm already failing at.
therapist: The fear of failing at one more thing makes complete sense given how much weight you're already carrying, and I want to gently name something — the fact that you're anticipating and problem-solving around obstacles before they happen is actually you protecting yourself, not evidence that you're failing. What if we reframed the reminder not as something you have to *feel* deeply every time, but simply as a small act of showing up for yourself, the same way you show up to work even on the scared days — some mornings it might land, others it might not, and both are okay? I'm curious, what would it look like to give yourself permission to try this imperfectly, without it counting as a failure if it doesn't work every single day?

client: Giving myself permission to do something imperfectly is actually really hard for me — I think I have this all-or-nothing thing where if I'm not doing it right every day, it means it's not working and I should just stop. When you put it in terms of showing up imperfectly the way I do with work, that framing does make a little more sense to me, because I don't quit my job on the days I'm struggling. I guess I could try to hold it that loosely, but I honestly don't know if I'll be able to catch myself when I start sliding into "this isn't working, forget it" mode.
therapist: You've just identified something really significant — that all-or-nothing thinking is actually one of the core patterns that keeps people stuck, and the fact that you can see it so clearly in yourself is genuinely meaningful progress. The work analogy you connected with is worth holding onto, because you already have living proof that imperfect showing up counts — you haven't quit your job on the hard days, and that's exactly the standard we're aiming for here, not perfection. When you notice that "this isn't working, forget it" voice starting up, what do you think it would take to treat it like a thought worth questioning rather than a fact worth obeying?

client: I think what it would take is actually remembering in that moment that the voice is a thought and not a fact, which sounds simple but feels really hard when you're inside it. It's like the voice is so loud and convincing that questioning it feels almost pointless, like arguing with someone who's already decided they're right. I guess the honest answer is I don't fully know how to do that yet, and I'm a little worried that's something I'd need a lot of practice at before it actually sticks.
therapist: The honesty in "I don't fully know how to do that yet" is actually exactly the right place to be — noticing that the voice feels louder than reason isn't a flaw in you, it's just how deeply practiced that pattern has become, and practice in the other direction is genuinely how it shifts over time. You're not behind or failing by not already knowing how to do this; you're at the very beginning of building a new skill, the same way you couldn't have shown up to your job on day one the way you do now. What do you think it might feel like, even just a little, to give yourself the same patience you'd give someone else who was learning something genuinely difficult for the first time?
